reading.rtitle: Reading a Diagnostic Study -- A Step 3 Guide
paras: THE QUESTION. A dermatology clinic wanted to know if dermoscopy finds melanoma better than the naked eye. Two hundred pigmented lesions were examined twice, once with each method, and every lesion went to biopsy. Biopsy was the reference standard: the most accurate test available, and the one the other two were compared with.

THE RESULTS. Forty lesions were melanomas. Dermoscopy found thirty-six of them, so its sensitivity was ninety percent. The naked eye found twenty-eight, a sensitivity of seventy percent. In other words, the visual exam missed twice as many melanomas as dermoscopy: eight against four. Specificity was closer: eighty-five percent with dermoscopy and eighty-two percent with the naked eye.

HOW PRECISE? The confidence interval for the sensitivity of dermoscopy was roughly seventy-seven to ninety-seven percent. It is wide, because forty melanomas is a small number. A bigger study would give a narrower interval and a more precise answer.

WHAT IT MEANS. In this clinic, the prevalence of melanoma among the lesions was twenty percent, which is much higher than in a general population. In a lower-prevalence setting, the same test would produce more false positives for every true melanoma. For the authors, the benefit of finding melanoma earlier outweighs the cost of the extra biopsies.

listenings.text: Students tell me biostatistics is the hardest part of Step 3, and it is usually because they try to memorize formulas. You need very few. What you need is to understand two numbers. Sensitivity tells you how well a test finds the people who have the disease. A very sensitive test rarely misses anybody, so when it is negative, you can rule the disease out with confidence. Specificity is the opposite: it tells you how well the test finds the people who do not have the disease. When a very specific test is positive, you can rule the disease in. Now, the question writers love one more idea: prevalence. The same test works differently in different places. In a specialist clinic, where the disease is common, a positive result is usually right. In the general population, where the disease is much less common, the same test gives you more false positives for every true case. So when you read a question, ask two things first: is this test more sensitive or more specific, and how common is the disease in this group?

Last year I presented a study at our journal club, and I was very excited about it. A new app claimed to be more accurate than dermatologists at finding melanoma. The sensitivity was ninety-five percent, which was higher than the sensitivity of the doctors in the study. I thought it was the most important paper of the year. Then my attending asked me two questions. How many melanomas were there? And what was the prevalence? I looked again. There were only thirty melanomas, so the confidence interval was very wide, roughly from eighty to ninety-nine percent. And almost half of the lesions in the study were melanomas, which is much higher than in a real clinic. In a normal population, the app would produce many more false positives. The study was not wrong, but it was much less impressive than the title. Since then, before I believe any result, I look at two things first: the size of the study and the prevalence.

extra_audio.text: This study compared dermoscopy with the naked eye for melanoma. Two hundred lesions were examined with both methods, and all of them went to biopsy. Dermoscopy was much more sensitive than the naked eye. Specificity was only slightly lower with the naked eye. The confidence interval was wide, because the study was small. In my opinion, the benefits of dermoscopy outweigh the cost.
